summary: Shows the security problems that come from allowing overlapping fragments in IPv6, and updates the base IPv6 specification to explicitly forbid them. Receivers must handle such packets as the document describes. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 fragments let a sender divide a datagram into smaller pieces for delivery. RFC 5722 forbids overlapping pieces because different systems could interpret the reconstructed data differently.

questions: why are overlapping fragments a security risk
what happens to overlapping ipv6 fragments
how do overlapping fragments bypass a firewall
subtitle: Forbid overlapping IPv6 fragments so reassembly cannot change what a firewall inspected.

tldr.problem: IPv6 fragmentation allowed pieces of a datagram to overlap. An attacker could use the overlap to make a firewall inspect different transport information from what the destination reconstructs.
tldr.mechanism: A sender MUST NOT create overlapping fragments. A receiver that detects one MUST silently discard the entire datagram.
tldr.outcome: The rule updates RFC 2460 and RFC 6946 later updates this RFC.

today: RFC 5722 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2009. It updates RFC 2460, and the unit metadata says RFC 6946 later updated it.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Fragments Need a Rule
sections.content:
IPv6 uses fragmentation when a packet will not fit within the path's maximum transmission unit. A sender divides the datagram, and the destination reassembles the fragments.

The base IPv6 specification did not prevent fragments from overlapping. This RFC explains the security consequences and updates the IPv6 rules to prohibit overlap.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender may split one IPv6 datagram into pieces, and the destination joins those pieces again. The pieces must not cover the same data, because that can make the final result ambiguous.

sections.title: Why a Firewall Can Miss the Attack
sections.content:
Some firewalls inspect fragments to detect attempts to overwrite transport headers and bypass inbound connection checks. An IPv4 defense recommends dropping fragments with offset 1.

That check is less effective for IPv6 because extension headers can occur before the TCP header in the fragmentable part. The TCP header may therefore appear at a different offset.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall may inspect only part of a fragmented packet. IPv6 extension headers can move the transport header, so a fixed offset check may not find the important fields.

sections.title: How Overlap Can Change a Packet
sections.content:
The RFC describes a first fragment containing an 80-octet Destination Options Header followed by a TCP header with SYN and ACK set. A stateful firewall may interpret it as a response to a connection begun from the trusted side and allow related fragments with the same Fragment Identification.

A second, overlapping fragment can replace part of the TCP header and set SYN while clearing ACK. After reassembly, the destination sees a connection request rather than the reply the firewall inspected. In IPv6, the overlap can also replace source or destination ports.
sections.plainLanguage: The first fragment can appear to be an allowed reply, while another fragment changes the TCP fields before reassembly. The destination may then receive a packet that the firewall did not actually approve.

sections.title: Required Sender and Receiver Behavior
sections.content:
An IPv6 node that sends a datagram requiring fragmentation MUST NOT create overlapping fragments. This is a requirement on the sender.

During reassembly, if any fragment overlaps another, the node MUST silently discard the entire datagram. This includes fragments already received and fragments that have not yet arrived. A node MAY count or raise alarms for these events.
sections.plainLanguage: Senders must make fragment ranges that do not overlap. If a receiver finds any overlap, it discards the whole datagram without replying.

sections.title: The Two-Fragment Example
sections.content:
The example uses two fragments with the same Identification value, aaaabbbb. The first fragment has offset 0 and the more-fragments bit set; it carries an 80-octet Destination Options Header before TCP.

The second fragment has offset 10 and the more-fragments bit cleared. Its data begins within the first fragment's TCP header, creating the overlap that can alter the flags seen after reassembly.
sections.plainLanguage: In the example, both fragments share an identification value, and their data ranges overlap. The receiver must reject the datagram rather than choose which fragment's bytes to keep.

viz.caption: The two rules for overlapping fragments

items.title: Sender
items.text: Must not create overlapping IPv6 fragments.

items.title: Receiver
items.text: Silently discards the complete datagram when fragments overlap.
